studies.title: Divergent impacts of explainable AI for dermatological diagnosis on clinicians versus lay people
studies.finding: Task: giving a top-three differential diagnosis from clinical photographs of skin conditions. The study focused on atopic dermatitis, pityriasis rosea, Lyme disease and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with images balanced across light and dark skin tones. AI system: a deep learning model trained to perform evenly across skin tones, shown with one of four kinds of explanation (prediction only, heatmap, similar example images, or a multimodal large language model's written explanation). Humans: 153 primary care physicians (PCPs) diagnosed each image first on their own and then again with AI help. The paper also tested 320 medical students on the same task and 623 lay people on a simpler melanoma-versus-mole task. Main result: without AI, PCPs had 11.5 ± 1.4% top-1 accuracy and 16.1 ± 1.8% top-3 accuracy; with AI suggestions, top-1 accuracy rose by 21.5% and top-3 by 43.5%. When the AI was wrong, the PCPs' final answers barely changed, but medical students and lay people relied on the AI more. The written LLM explanations helped PCPs the least. Main limitation: this was a simplified online experiment with only 12 images per participant and no patient history. The authors also chose the images on purpose so the AI was right about 79% of the time, which does not reflect how the model would behave in real use.

studies.title: Interval cancer, sensitivity, and specificity comparing AI-supported mammography screening with standard double reading without AI in the MASAI study: a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, population-based, screening-accuracy trial
studies.ai_system: Transpara, used to triage exams to single or double reading and to support detection
studies.humans: Screening radiologists in the Swedish programme. Arms: AI-supported screening vs standard double reading without AI. 105,934 women randomised 1:1 (53,043 vs 52,872).
studies.finding: The primary outcome was the interval cancer rate after at least two years of follow-up. It was 1·55 (95% CI 1·23–1·92) per 1000 with AI-supported screening and 1·76 (1·42–2·15) per 1000 with standard double reading, a proportion ratio of 0·88 that met non-inferiority. The AI arm had fewer invasive (75 vs 89), T2+ (38 vs 48) and non-luminal A (43 vs 59) interval cancers, and the authors report higher sensitivity.
studies.limitation: The primary analysis was powered for non-inferiority, not superiority, and was run in one Swedish screening programme with one AI product.

studies.title: Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial
studies.ai_system: Microsoft Dragon Ambient eXperience (DAX) Copilot and Nabla ambient AI scribes
studies.humans: 238 outpatient physicians from 14 specialties at one academic health system, randomised 1:1:1 to DAX, Nabla or usual care
studies.finding: The primary outcome was the change from baseline in log writing time-in-note. Nabla users had a 9.5% decrease (95% CI −17.2% to −1.8%; P=0.02) versus control, while DAX users showed no significant change (−1.7%; 95% CI −9.4% to +5.9%; P=0.66). Both scribes improved Mini-Z scores (DAX +2.83; Nabla +2.69).
studies.limitation: Scribes were used in only about 30% of visits (33.5% DAX, 29.5% Nabla) over a two-month period at a single health system.

studies.title: Performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
studies.design: six-experiment comparison including blinded evaluation of real emergency department cases
studies.ai_system: OpenAI o1 series (o1-preview), compared with GPT-4 and physician baselines
studies.humans: Hundreds of physicians at different training levels across the experiments; two attending physicians in the real-world emergency department experiment
studies.finding: o1 was compared with physicians on diagnosis and management reasoning, from published vignettes to 76 real emergency department cases at three decision points. At initial triage, o1 placed the correct or a very close diagnosis in 67.1% of cases, compared with 55.3% and 50.0% for the two attending physicians. Across experiments the authors report that the model outperformed physicians and older models.
studies.limitation: The real-world arm compared the model with only two physicians on 76 text-only cases from one centre, and several tasks used curated vignettes.

studies.title: Large language model diagnostic assistance for physicians in a lower-middle-income country: a randomized controlled trial
studies.design: single-blind randomised controlled trial with clinical vignettes
studies.humans: 60 licensed physicians in Pakistan (58 completed), all after a 20-hour AI-literacy course
studies.finding: On up to 6 vignettes, physicians with LLM access plus usual resources had a mean diagnostic reasoning score of 71.4%, versus 42.6% with usual resources alone. The adjusted difference was 27.5 percentage points (95% CI 22.8 to 32.2), and time per case was similar. In an exploratory analysis the LLM alone beat LLM-assisted physicians by 11.5 percentage points (95% CI 5.5 to 17.5).
studies.limitation: Small vignette-based study of physicians given intensive AI-literacy training, which may not generalise to untrained clinicians or real patients.

studies.title: Automation Bias in Large Language Model–Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among Physicians Trained in AI Literacy — A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT-4o, with deliberately erroneous suggestions in 3 of 6 vignettes for the treatment arm
studies.humans: 44 physicians in Pakistan who had completed a 20-hour AI-literacy programme
studies.finding: Physicians diagnosed six vignettes. The treatment arm got deliberately wrong LLM suggestions in some cases; the control arm got error-free ones. Mean composite diagnostic accuracy was 73.3% with wrong suggestions versus 84.9% in controls, an adjusted reduction of 14.0 percentage points (95% CI −18.9 to −9.1; P<0.0001). Top-choice accuracy was 76.1% versus 90.5%.
studies.limitation: Small vignette trial in which LLM errors were planted by the investigators, so the error rate does not reflect real-world LLM output.

studies.title: Computer-Assisted Colonoscopy in High–Adenoma Detection Rate Settings in a High-Risk Population: A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.humans: Senior and junior endoscopists in a high adenoma detection rate setting, performing 1356 randomised colonoscopies
studies.finding: CAD-assisted colonoscopy met non-inferiority for adenoma detection rate against standard colonoscopy (58.5% vs 53.3%), but superiority was not statistically significant overall. Gains appeared only in an exploratory FIT-positive subgroup (65.3% vs 57.4%; P=.02), driven mainly by diminutive adenomas, and CAD led to more intensive surveillance recommendations.
studies.limitation: Enrolment of 1356 fell short of the planned 1480, and the surrogate endpoint (ADR) does not show any effect on cancer prevention.

studies.title: Artificial intelligence assisted colorectal lesion detection in private practices a randomized controlled study
studies.design: prospective multicentre randomised controlled trial in private practices
studies.humans: Highly experienced endoscopists in private endoscopy centres across Germany doing screening and surveillance colonoscopy (number of endoscopists not confirmed)
studies.finding: The primary endpoint was mean adenoma detection rate. It was 32.9% with traditional colonoscopy and 34.5% with computer-aided colonoscopy (p = 0.656), with no significant difference in the intention-to-treat analysis.
studies.limitation: Control-group ADR was higher than assumed in the power calculation, so the trial may have been underpowered to detect a small benefit.

studies.title: Randomized Controlled Trial of Large Language Model–Assisted Diagnostic Accuracy in Nephrology
studies.design: online randomised open-label parallel-group trial (research letter)
studies.humans: 97 residents and board-certified physicians, mostly nephrologists and mostly French, giving 556 case evaluations
studies.finding: On complex open-ended nephrology vignettes, top-3 diagnostic accuracy was 57.5% with AI versus 37.2% without (adjusted OR 2.8, 95% CI 1.5–5.2). Top-1 accuracy was 51.5% versus 33.0% (adjusted OR 2.7). GPT-5 alone reached 77.1% on the same benchmark, well above AI-assisted clinicians.
studies.limitation: Short research letter on fixed vignettes, not powered for subgroups, with a largely French volunteer sample.

studies.title: Diagnostic capability of large language models in critically ill patients: a prospective single-centre study comparing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini with emergency physicians
studies.design: prospective single-centre observational diagnostic agreement study
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro
studies.humans: Emergency physicians caring for 180 critically ill emergency department patients (number of physicians not stated)
studies.finding: Diagnoses were compared stage by stage on real critically ill ED cases. Physicians had the reference diagnosis in their top-5 preliminary list in 83.9% of cases and their top-3 differential in 98.3%, significantly better than every LLM (all p < 0.001).
studies.limitation: The reference diagnosis was the physicians' own final diagnosis, which biases the comparison in the physicians' favour.

studies.title: Comparing Ophthalmologist and Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions
studies.design: retrospective cross-sectional comparison of written responses
studies.humans: 41 board-certified ophthalmologists answering on the AAO 'Ask an Ophthalmologist' forum (250 questions sampled)
studies.finding: Ophthalmologist evaluators rated the accuracy of answers to patient eye-health questions on a 7-point Likert scale. ChatGPT and ophthalmologist answers had similar mean accuracy (5.8 [SD=1.1] vs 5.5 [SD=1.1], p=0.07), and evaluators preferred ChatGPT in 49.5% of cases. Ophthalmologist answers were easier to read (grade 11.0 vs 12.7, p<0.001).
studies.limitation: Forum answers were written asynchronously by volunteers years earlier, so they may not reflect clinicians' best effort or real clinical communication.

studies.title: Improving Diagnostic And Management Accuracy In Hard-To-Diagnose Pigmented Skin Lesions With Interactive And Interpretable AI Assistant For Dermatoscopy: Results From A Two-Phase Reader Study
studies.finding: Task: classify dermoscopic images of pigmented skin lesions into seven diagnosis groups and choose what to do next (dismiss, biopsy or treat, or follow up). AI: idea®, an interactive decision-support platform that detects and highlights dermoscopic patterns and, once the physician has reviewed them, gives a rule-based diagnosis grounded in established dermoscopic criteria. Humans: 16 physicians with proven dermoscopy experience read 208 images, first without the tool and then, after a washout of at least 14 days, with it. On the 49 hard lesions (cases misclassified or read with low confidence without the tool), the share correctly called malignant or benign rose from 50.6% without AI to 69.3% with AI (p < 0.001), correct diagnosis from 28.3% to 45.0% (p < 0.001), and correct management from 53.0% to 64.8% (p = 0.02). The biggest limitation: this was a non-randomised, before-and-after reader study on images rather than real patients. The second phase was deliberately weighted toward hard lesions, and the key results apply to that subset, not to every lesion.

studies.title: Impact of LLM assistance on physician decision-making: a multi-country randomized controlled trial
studies.finding: Physicians worked through standardised clinical vignettes to test their clinical decision-making. Physicians given access to GPT-4o were compared with physicians who had no AI access. The parallel-group randomised trial enrolled 249 physicians in Indonesia, Kenya and the Netherlands. Physicians with GPT-4o access scored higher on the vignettes in every country. The gap was 18 percentage points in Kenya (95% CI 12.7 to 23.2, p < 0.001), 10.7 percentage points in Indonesia (95% CI 5.7 to 15.7, p < 0.001) and 7.2 percentage points in the Netherlands (95% CI 3.7 to 10.7, p < 0.001). The main limitation is that this was done with written cases under controlled conditions, not with real patients. The control group was also not allowed to use the internet or clinical guidelines, and harms were not assessed. The paper is an early peer-reviewed version that may still be edited before the final version.

studies.title: Large language models improve physician accuracy but lead to false reliance
studies.finding: In this preprint, physicians answered clinical cases with and without help from an AI assistant. The AI was CORA, an agentic large language model built by researchers led by the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, which pulls in sources and shows citations for its answers. Among the 46 physicians in the study, accuracy rose from 70.8% unaided to 82.6% with CORA. The citations cut both ways: when they appeared to back a correct answer, physicians took the advice 76.9% of the time, up from 34%, but when they appeared to back a wrong answer, physicians' resistance to that answer fell from 92% to 34.8%. The most important limitations are that the preprint has not been peer reviewed and that 46 physicians were tested on study cases, not on real patients in live care.

studies.title: Radiologists, LLMs fail at spotting AI-generated chest x-rays
studies.source: AuntMinnie (reporting a study in the Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine)
studies.finding: The task was sorting 160 chest X-rays into real (40) or AI-generated (120, made by three different image-generation pipelines). Three large language models (Gemini 3.5 Flash, GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) were compared with four human readers from a Seoul National University Hospital team: two radiologists and two general practitioners. On the main measure, balanced accuracy, the top performers were Gemini 3.5 Flash at 77.9% and one radiologist at 75.8%, with no statistically significant difference between them, while the general practitioners performed near chance. Humans were better at spotting images made by diffusion models (82% to 100% vs 32% to 72% for the LLMs), and the LLMs were better at correctly calling real images real (90% to 100% vs 50% to 100%). The main limitation is size: only four human readers and 160 images, on a task about checking image authenticity rather than making a diagnosis. These figures come from a trade-press report of the peer-reviewed paper.

studies.title: AI-based clinician decision support system for diagnosis of inherited retinal diseases: a multicenter, randomized trial
studies.finding: The task was to predict which of 17 genotype categories caused a suspected inherited retinal disease, using retinal images (colour fundus photographs and OCT scans), before genetic test results were available. The AI was Retina4IRD, a Vision Transformer tool pretrained with RETFound. In a multicentre randomised controlled trial, 300 patients were randomised 1:1 to retinal specialists working with Retina4IRD or specialists working alone; 295 had sequencing results and were analysed. The abstract does not say how many specialists took part. On the primary outcome, top-5 genetic accuracy, the AI-assisted arm scored 88.5% and the specialist-only arm 67.3% (P < 0.001), and top-1 accuracy was 37.8% versus 22.4%. The most important limitation is that the trial measured whether the predicted genotype category matched sequencing, not patient outcomes; the finding that management decisions were better with AI came from a post hoc analysis.

studies.title: Comparative Cost of Care Recommended by Large Language Models versus Treating Physicians
studies.finding: The task was writing an assessment and plan from the clinical presentation in de-identified outpatient and emergency department notes. The orders in each plan were then priced using the 2026 Medicare fee schedules. The AI side was 24 systems (20 general-purpose large language models and 4 specialized medical systems), each given the same 200 cases. The human comparison was the plan actually documented by each case's treating physician; the number of physicians is not stated in the authors' public materials. On the main measure, cost of care, a Nature research highlight of the paper reports that LLM-suggested plans were three times as costly as physicians' plans, driven by more tests, referrals and medications. The most important limitation is that this was a retrospective study of documented notes rather than real-time care, and higher cost alone does not show whether the extra orders helped or harmed patients.

studies.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
studies.finding: The task was step-by-step diagnosis. Researchers turned 629 published NEJM case records and emergency department encounters into interactive cases where you ask questions and order tests, and each test adds to an estimated cost. The AI was Microsoft's Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), running on GPT-5. It was compared with practising generalist physicians, who worked through a 56-case subset of the complex NEJM cases. Depending on its test budget, the AI reached the correct diagnosis in 79.6% to 84.5% of cases. Physicians averaged 22.3% without reference tools and 36.1% with them, and even the best physician (51.8%) was beaten by the AI on both accuracy and cost. The main limitation is that these were simulated, text-only cases built from past records, not real patients. The AI could not examine anyone, the cases were hard ones given to generalists, and the authors, who work at Microsoft, say it still needs testing in real clinical practice.

studies.title: Clinicians vs. artificial intelligence in patient outcome prediction in the intensive care unit
studies.finding: The task was predicting outcomes for ICU patients: in-hospital and 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, delirium, and ICU and hospital length of stay. The AI was a set of prediction models trained on 46,631 ICU admissions. In the retrospective arm, seven clinicians predicted outcomes for 990 admissions from patient data alone. In the prospective arm, clinicians made predictions for 238 admissions during active care, while the AI worked from data extracted for the same admissions. The preprint version reports that 75 clinicians made at least one prediction, across 15 adult ICUs in Alberta, Canada. The abstract reports the results as direct comparisons rather than headline numbers. In the retrospective arm, AI generally beat individual clinicians, but the pooled predictions of all seven clinicians beat the AI. In the prospective arm, subspecialised physicians generally beat the AI, while physicians in training and nurses generally did worse than it. Combining clinician and AI predictions often gave the best results. The main limitation is that the real-world prospective arm was small (238 admissions) and confined to one Canadian province's ICUs, and the AI saw extracted data rather than the bedside picture the clinicians had.

studies.title: Performance of Clinical AI System and Physicians and Frontier Language Models in primary care diagnostics
studies.finding: The task was to run adaptive primary-care consultations, asking questions before choosing a diagnosis, a workup and initial treatment, across 150 synthetic Polish-language cases. The AI was Doctorina, a clinical AI system, which was also compared with four standalone frontier language models. The human comparison group was eight physicians. Doctorina's Top-1 diagnostic concordance was 82.0% against 57.0% for the physicians (difference 25.0 percentage points; 95% CI 17.7–32.7), and its primary-or-reference-differential concordance was 97.3% against 85.0%. Across 149 case pairs, normalized workup scores were 89.4 against 66.9 and treatment scores were 83.7 against 61.2. The main limitation is that the cases were synthetic consultations, not real patients, and only eight physicians took part. This is also a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and its authors include Doctorina's co-founder and staff.

studies.title: Clinician-centered evaluation of large language model-generated discharge summaries for longer hospitalizations
studies.design: Paired blinded comparison of LLM-generated vs human-authored discharge summaries
studies.ai_system: A large language model; the specific model could not be confirmed from the abstract
studies.humans: Human-authored discharge summaries from 60 Internal Medicine hospitalisations lasting 7 to 21 days, rated in pairs by hospitalists and primary care physicians (number of raters not confirmed)
studies.finding: Clinician reviewers compared LLM-generated and human-authored discharge summaries for 60 longer Internal Medicine stays. They preferred the LLM-generated summaries for 95% of encounters and rated them higher for quality, readability, factuality and completeness. PCPs rated the LLM summaries as better for understanding and communicating hospital care and for follow-up care; of 31 radiology incidental findings the LLM identified, 93.5% were rated factually correct and 87.1% appropriate for reporting.
studies.limitation: Only 60 hospitalisations from one internal medicine setting were used, and the outcome is clinicians' ratings and preferences, not downstream patient outcomes or errors in care.

changes.text: This edition adds ten studies, including the first randomised trial on real patients outside screening and endoscopy, in inherited retinal disease, a multi-country trial of LLM help on written cases, and new evidence that citations can drive false reliance on AI. It also adds studies on the cost of AI-written care plans, step-by-step diagnosis on simulated cases, ICU outcome prediction, LLM-written discharge summaries, dermoscopy decision support and detection of AI-generated X-rays, which broaden the picture beyond diagnosis while keeping it mixed.

This is the first edition. It covers 11 studies published between November 2025 and August 2026: screening and procedural trials in mammography and colonoscopy, LLM diagnostic trials on vignettes and real emergency department cases, an automation-bias trial, ambient scribes, patient communication and AI-assisted skin diagnosis.

title: AI vs Human: how AI is changing what physicians can do
summary: The strongest evidence still comes from randomised trials in which clinicians use AI on real patients. AI-supported mammography screening was at least as safe as double reading [S2], and AI help raised retinal specialists' accuracy in predicting the genetic cause of inherited retinal disease [S16], but colonoscopy detection aids showed no clear overall gain [S7][S8] and ambient scribes gave mixed results [S3]. On written or simulated cases, large language models (LLMs) raised physicians' scores in randomised trials across several countries [S5][S9][S13][S14], and the models alone often scored higher still [S5][S9][S18][S20]. Real-patient comparisons remain split [S4][S10][S19], wrong or citation-backed AI advice can pull physicians toward errors [S6][S14], and one study found LLM care plans about three times as costly as physicians' plans [S17].
key_findings: In a population-based trial of 105,934 women, AI-supported mammography screening was non-inferior to standard double reading on interval cancers, at 1.55 versus 1.76 per 1000 [S2].

In a multicentre randomised trial of 300 patients, retinal specialists helped by an AI tool predicted the genetic cause of inherited retinal disease more often than specialists alone (top-5 accuracy 88.5% vs 67.3%), though patient outcomes were not measured [S16].
Two randomised colonoscopy trials found no significant overall rise in adenoma detection with computer-aided detection [S7][S8].

On written cases, LLM access raised physicians' scores in randomised trials in Pakistan, France, Kenya, Indonesia and the Netherlands, with the smallest gain in the Netherlands (7.2 points) [S5][S9][S13].
On written cases the LLM working alone often outscored physicians who had the same LLM's help, so simply giving physicians the tool did not capture all of its performance [S5][S9].
Wrong AI advice lowered physicians' accuracy, by 14 points with planted errors [S6], and citations attached to wrong answers cut physicians' resistance to those answers from 92% to 34.8% [S14].

On real patients the picture is split: an LLM beat two attending physicians at emergency triage [S4], emergency physicians beat four LLMs on critically ill patients [S10], and in ICU outcome prediction subspecialists beat the AI while trainees and nurses did worse than it [S19].

sections.heading: AI on its own against clinicians
paragraphs: The head-to-head studies where AI comes out clearly ahead mostly use written or simulated cases. On 56 complex published case records turned into step-by-step puzzles, a GPT-5-based system reached the right diagnosis in 79.6% to 84.5% of cases, while generalist physicians averaged 22.3% without reference tools and 36.1% with them [S18]. A commercial primary-care system beat eight physicians on 150 synthetic Polish consultations (top-1 concordance 82.0% vs 57.0%) [S20]. Both deserve caution: the cases were not real patients, the AI could not examine anyone, the first was run by the system's developer, and the second is a preprint with the company's co-founder and staff among its authors [S18][S20].

On real patients the results disagree. An LLM placed the correct or a very close diagnosis at triage in 67.1% of 76 emergency cases at one centre, against 55.3% and 50.0% for two attending physicians [S4]. In 180 critically ill emergency patients at another single centre, physicians were significantly better than every one of four LLMs, although the reference diagnosis was the physicians' own final diagnosis, which favours them [S10]. In ICU outcome prediction, AI generally beat individual clinicians on retrospective data but lost to the pooled judgement of all seven clinicians; during live care, subspecialists generally beat it and trainees and nurses did not [S19].

Comparisons beyond diagnosis also cut both ways. In a retrospective study of 200 outpatient and emergency notes, plans written by 24 AI systems were reported to cost about three times as much as the treating physicians' plans, though whether the extra orders helped or harmed patients was not assessed [S17]. On written tasks, AI matched or was preferred to clinicians in answering patient eye questions [S11] and in writing discharge summaries [S21]. A small study found the best LLM and the best radiologist similarly able to spot AI-generated chest X-rays, while general practitioners performed near chance [S15].

sections.heading: Clinicians working with AI
paragraphs: The firmest evidence on real patients comes from a few randomised trials, and they do not all point the same way. AI-supported mammography screening in one Swedish programme was non-inferior to double reading, with fewer invasive interval cancers in the AI arm (75 vs 89) [S2]. A multicentre trial in 300 patients found that retinal specialists with AI help predicted the genotype category of inherited retinal disease more accurately (top-1 37.8% vs 22.4%); better management decisions were seen only in a post hoc analysis [S16]. Against these, two colonoscopy trials found no significant overall gain in adenoma detection [S7][S8], and an ambient scribe trial found one product cut note-writing time by 9.5% while the other did not [S3].

On written cases, randomised trials consistently show physicians scoring higher with an LLM: by 27.5 points in Pakistan [S5], from 37.2% to 57.5% top-3 accuracy in nephrology [S9], from 70.8% to 82.6% with a citing AI assistant [S14], and by 7.2 to 18 points across Kenya, Indonesia and the Netherlands [S13]. The multi-country trial's control group could not use the internet or guidelines, which may inflate the gap [S13], and one of these studies is a preprint with 46 physicians [S14]. In two trials the model alone scored higher than the assisted physicians [S5][S9].

sections.heading: Reading images and other pattern tasks
paragraphs: Imaging and pattern tasks give the most real-world trial evidence, and it is mixed. Screening mammography [S2] and genetic prediction from retinal images [S16] showed gains or non-inferiority on real patients, while colonoscopy detection did not show a clear overall benefit; one trial saw gains only in an exploratory subgroup, mostly from very small adenomas, alongside more intensive surveillance recommendations [S7], and the other may have been underpowered [S8].

In dermatology the evidence is from image-based reader studies, not clinic. In an online experiment with 153 primary care physicians, AI suggestions raised top-1 accuracy by 21.5% and top-3 by 43.5% from a low baseline (11.5% and 16.1%), but the images were chosen so the AI was right about 79% of the time and there was no patient history [S1]. In a before-and-after study of 16 experienced dermoscopists, an interpretable AI tool raised correct malignant-or-benign calls on 49 hard lesions from 50.6% to 69.3% and correct management from 53.0% to 64.8%; this was not randomised and the result applies to the hard subset only [S12].

sections.heading: Diagnosis, reasoning and management
paragraphs: Diagnosis is where LLMs have been tested most, nearly always on written or simulated cases [S5][S9][S13][S14][S18][S20]. These studies show sizeable score gains with AI help and strong standalone model performance, but they test reading and reasoning about a prepared case, not taking a history, examining a patient or following them over time. The two real-patient emergency studies reach opposite conclusions, and each has a small or biased comparison [S4][S10].

Management is less studied. AI-assisted physicians chose correct management more often on hard skin lesions [S12], and a primary-care preprint reported higher workup and treatment scores for its AI on synthetic cases [S20]. The cost study is a counterweight: LLM plans ordered more tests, referrals and medications than treating physicians did [S17]. Higher scores on prepared cases and higher costs on real notes have not yet been tested against patient outcomes in the same study.

sections.heading: Communication and documentation
paragraphs: One randomised trial of ambient scribes at a single health system found a modest time saving with one product, none with the other, and small improvements in a burnout-related score with both; the scribes were used in only about 30% of visits [S3]. Clinician reviewers preferred LLM-written discharge summaries for 95% of 60 longer hospital stays and rated them higher on quality, factuality and completeness, though the study measured ratings, not errors in care [S21].

For patient questions, ChatGPT answers to eye-health questions were rated similarly accurate to ophthalmologists' forum answers but were harder to read [S11]. The comparison used old volunteer forum answers, which may not reflect clinicians' best effort [S11].

sections.heading: Training, examinations and skill
paragraphs: Experience changes how people use AI. When the dermatology AI was wrong, primary care physicians barely changed their answers, but medical students and lay people followed it more [S1]. In ICU prediction during live care, subspecialised physicians generally beat the AI while physicians in training and nurses did worse than it [S19]. Radiologists, but not general practitioners, could tell AI-generated chest X-rays from real ones, in a study with only four human readers [S15].

Training in AI use does not remove the risk of being misled: physicians who had completed a 20-hour AI-literacy course still lost accuracy when given wrong suggestions [S6]. No study in the register tests AI in medical examinations or tracks how trainees' skills develop over time with AI.

sections.heading: Risks: over-reliance, lost skill and bias
paragraphs: Over-reliance is now shown in two independent settings. Planted errors in LLM suggestions cut physicians' accuracy by 14 points in a vignette trial [S6]. In a preprint, citations shown with an AI's answers raised acceptance of correct advice from 34% to 76.9% but cut resistance to wrong advice from 92% to 34.8% [S14]. In dermatology, trainees and lay people followed wrong AI answers more than primary care physicians did [S1]. Written LLM explanations helped physicians the least of four explanation types [S1].

Other risks appear less directly. More tests and referrals in AI-written plans [S17] and more intensive surveillance after AI-assisted colonoscopy [S7] suggest AI can push care toward more intervention, with benefit unproven. On bias, a dermatology model trained to perform evenly across skin tones was tested on images balanced for light and dark skin [S1], but no study here compares performance across patient groups in real care. No study in the register measures whether clinicians lose skill after relying on AI.

sections.heading: Where this is heading
paragraphs: This section is interpretation rather than direct evidence. The evidence base is moving from single-model vignette tests toward trials with real patients outside screening [S16], multi-country trials [S13] and studies that look at cost [S17][S18], but most diagnostic work still rests on prepared cases [S5][S9][S13][S18][S20].

Two trends stand out. First, the repeated finding that the model alone outscores assisted physicians on written cases [S5][S9], together with ICU results where combining clinician and AI predictions often did best [S19], points to how humans and AI are combined as the open design question, not whether the AI is capable. Second, evidence that confident-looking AI output, including citations, can draw physicians into errors [S6][S14] suggests that how AI shows its reasoning matters as much as its accuracy. The register does not support predictions about patient outcomes, since almost no study here measured them.

open_questions: Do the large gains on written and simulated cases carry over to diagnosis and management with real patients in routine care?
Do any of these tools change patient outcomes, such as cancers prevented, harms avoided or deaths, rather than surrogate measures like detection rates, genotype accuracy or clinician ratings?
How should AI output be shown to clinicians so that they take correct advice but reject wrong advice, given that citations and explanations can increase false reliance?
